Muslims, Jews and Hindus do not consume pork and it had seemed inconsistent with the purpose of bringing together
persons of different faiths, though after the complaints raised by the Orthodox community a pork alternative was added.
Disease in pork
Pork is known to carry some diseases such as <color=#3366CC>pork tapeworm</color> and trichinosis and pigbel, thus uncooked or
undercooked pork can be dangerous to consume, although raw pork products are sometimes still consumed in <color=#3366CC>Central</color>
<color=#3366CC>European</color> and <color=#3366CC>Eastern European</color> countries of which the Eastern European countries are believed to have a higher risk
of trichinosis.
Undercooked or untreated pork may harbour pathogens, or can be recontaminated after cooking if left exposed for a
long period of time. In one instance, the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) detected <color=#3366CC>Listeria monocytogenes</color> in
460 lb of Polidori brand fully cooked pork sausage crumbles, although no one was made ill from consumption of the
product. The FSIS has previously stated that listeria and other microorganisms must be "...destroyed by proper
handling and thorough cooking to an internal temperature of 160 °F," and that other microorganisms, such as <color=#3366CC>E. coli</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Salmonella</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Staphylococcus aureus</color> can be found in inadequately cooked pork, poultry, and other meats. The
FSIS, a part of the USDA, currently recommends cooking ground pork to 160 °F and whole cuts to 145 °F followed by a
3-minute rest.
Pigs can be carriers of various helminths, such as <color=#3366CC>roundworms</color>, pinworms, hookworms. One of the more common is
<color=#3366CC>Taenia solium</color>, a type of <color=#3366CC>tapeworm</color>, which may transplant to the intestines of humans after consuming undercooked
meat. Raw and undercooked pork can also cause other diseases, such as <color=#3366CC>toxoplasmosis</color>.
Although not a common cause of illness, Yersinia enterocolitica—which causes gastroenteritis—is present in various
foods, but is most frequently caused by eating uncooked or undercooked pork and can grow in refrigerated conditions.
The bacteria can be killed by heat. Nearly all outbreaks in the US have been traced to pork.
Pork may be the reservoir responsible for sporadic, locally acquired cases of acute <color=#3366CC>hepatitis E</color> (HEV) reported in
regions with relatively mild climates. It has been found to transmit between swine and humans.
Trichinosis, also called trichinellosis, or trichiniasis, is a <color=#3366CC>parasitic disease</color> caused by eating raw or undercooked pork
infected with the <color=#3366CC>larvae</color> of a species of roundworm Trichinella spiralis, commonly called the trichina worm. Infection was
once very common, but is now rare in the <color=#3366CC>developed world</color>. From 2002 to 2007, an annual average of 11 cases per
year were reported in the United States; the majority were from consuming wild game or the source was unknown. The
number of cases has decreased because of legislation prohibiting the feeding of raw meat garbage to hogs, increased
commercial and home freezing of pork, and the public awareness of the danger of eating raw or undercooked pork or
wild game products.

Ether

In <color=#3366CC>organic chemistry</color>, ethers are a class of <color=#3366CC>compounds</color> that contain an ether <color=#3366CC>group</color>, a single <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color> atom bonded to two
separate carbon atoms, each part of an organyl group (e.g., alkyl or aryl). They have the general formula R\sO\sR′,
where R and R′ represent the organyl groups. Ethers can again be classified into two varieties: if the organyl groups are
the same on both sides of the oxygen atom, then it is a simple or symmetrical ether, whereas if they are different, the
ethers are called mixed or unsymmetrical ethers. A typical example of the first group is the <color=#3366CC>solvent</color> and <color=#3366CC>anaesthetic</color>
<color=#3366CC>diethyl ether</color>, commonly referred to simply as "ether" (CH3\sCH2\sO\sCH2\sCH3). Ethers are common in organic
chemistry and even more prevalent in <color=#3366CC>biochemistry</color>, as they are common linkages in <color=#3366CC>carbohydrates</color> and <color=#3366CC>lignin</color>.
History
Ethers were first isolated by Pierre-François-Guillaume Boullay and his son in the early 19th century.
Structure and bonding
Ethers feature bent C\sO\sC linkages. In <color=#3366CC>dimethyl ether</color>, the <color=#3366CC>bond angle</color> is 111° and C–O distances are 141 pm. The
barrier to rotation about the C–O bonds is low. The bonding of oxygen in ethers, alcohols, and water is similar. In the
language of <color=#3366CC>valence bond theory</color>, the hybridization at oxygen is sp3.
Ethers can be symmetrical of the type ROR or unsymmetrical of the type ROR'. Examples of the former are <color=#3366CC>dimethyl</color>
<color=#3366CC>ether</color>, <color=#3366CC>diethyl ether</color>, dipropyl ether etc. Illustrative unsymmetrical ethers are anisole (methoxybenzene) and
dimethoxyethane.
Vinyl- and acetylenic ethers
Vinyl- and acetylenic ethers are far less common than alkyl or aryl ethers. Vinylethers, often called enol ethers, are
important intermediates in <color=#3366CC>organic synthesis</color>. Acetylenic ethers are especially rare. Di-tert-butoxyacetylene is the most
common example of this rare class of compounds.
Nomenclature
In the <color=#3366CC>IUPAC Nomenclature</color> system, ethers are named using the general formula "alkoxyalkane", for example
CH3–CH2–O–CH3 is methoxyethane. If the ether is part of a more-complex molecule, it is described as an alkoxy
substituent, so –OCH3 would be considered a "methoxy-" group. The simpler alkyl radical is written in front, so
CH3–O–CH2CH3 would be given as methoxy(CH3O)ethane(CH2CH3).
Trivial names
IUPAC rules are often not followed for simple ethers. The trivial names for simple ethers (i.e., those with none or few
other functional groups) are a composite of the two substituents followed by "ether". For example, ethyl methyl ether
(CH3OC2H5), diphenylether (C6H5OC6H5). As for other organic compounds, very common ethers acquired names
before rules for nomenclature were formalized. Diethyl ether is simply called ether, but was once called sweet oil of
vitriol. Methyl phenyl ether is anisole, because it was originally found in <color=#3366CC>aniseed</color>. The <color=#3366CC>aromatic</color> ethers include furans.
Acetals (-alkoxy ethers R–CH(–OR)–O–R) are another class of ethers with characteristic properties.
Polyethers
Polyethers are generally <color=#3366CC>polymers</color> containing ether linkages in their main chain. The term <color=#3366CC>polyol</color> generally refers to
polyether polyols with one or more functional end-groups such as a hydroxyl group. The term "oxide" or other terms are
used for high molar mass polymer when end-groups no longer affect polymer properties.
Crown ethers are cyclic polyethers. Some toxins produced by <color=#3366CC>dinoflagellates</color> such as brevetoxin and ciguatoxin are
extremely large and are known as cyclic or ladder polyethers.
The phenyl ether polymers are a class of <color=#3366CC>aromatic</color> polyethers containing aromatic cycles in their main chain: polyphenyl
ether (PPE) and poly(p-phenylene oxide) (PPO).
Related compounds
Many classes of compounds with C–O–C linkages are not considered ethers: <color=#3366CC>Esters</color> (R–C(=O)–O–R′), hemiacetals
(R–CH(–OH)–O–R′), carboxylic acid anhydrides (RC(=O)–O–C(=O)R′).
There are compounds which, instead of <color=#3366CC>C</color> in the C\sO\sC linkage, contain heavier <color=#3366CC>group 14</color> <color=#3366CC>chemical elements</color> (e.g.,

<color=#3366CC>Si</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ge</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sn</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pb</color>). Such compounds are considered ethers as well. Examples of such ethers are silyl enol ethers
R3Si\sO\sCR\dCR2 (containing the Si\sO\sC linkage), disiloxane H3Si\sO\sSiH3 (the other name of this compound is
disilyl ether, containing the Si\sO\sSi linkage) and stannoxanes R3Sn\sO\sSnR3 (containing the Sn\sO\sSn linkage).
Physical properties
Ethers have <color=#3366CC>boiling points</color> similar to those of the analogous <color=#3366CC>alkanes</color>. Simple ethers are generally colorless.
Reactions
The C-O bonds that comprise simple ethers are strong. They are unreactive toward all but the strongest bases.
Although generally of low chemical <color=#3366CC>reactivity</color>, they are more reactive than <color=#3366CC>alkanes</color>.
Specialized ethers such as <color=#3366CC>epoxides</color>, ketals, and acetals are unrepresentative classes of ethers and are discussed in
separate articles. Important reactions are listed below.
Cleavage
Although ethers resist hydrolysis, they are cleaved by hydrobromic acid and hydroiodic acid. <color=#3366CC>Hydrogen chloride</color> cleaves
ethers only slowly. Methyl ethers typically afford methyl halides: ROCH3 + HBr CH3Br + ROH These reactions proceed
via onium intermediates, i.e. [RO(H)CH3]+Br.
Some ethers undergo rapid cleavage with boron tribromide (even <color=#3366CC>aluminium chloride</color> is used in some cases) to give the
alkyl halide. Depending on the substituents, some ethers can be cleaved with a variety of reagents, e.g. strong base.
Despite these difficulties the chemical <color=#3366CC>paper pulping</color> processes are based on cleavage of ether bonds in the <color=#3366CC>lignin</color>.
Peroxide formation
When stored in the presence of air or oxygen, ethers tend to form <color=#3366CC>explosive</color> peroxides, such as diethyl ether
hydroperoxide. The reaction is accelerated by light, metal catalysts, and <color=#3366CC>aldehydes</color>. In addition to avoiding storage
conditions likely to form peroxides, it is recommended, when an ether is used as a solvent, not to distill it to dryness, as
any peroxides that may have formed, being less volatile than the original ether, will become concentrated in the last few
drops of liquid. The presence of peroxide in old samples of ethers may be detected by shaking them with freshly
prepared solution of a ferrous sulfate followed by addition of KSCN. Appearance of blood red color indicates presence
of peroxides. The dangerous properties of ether peroxides are the reason that diethyl ether and other peroxide forming
ethers like <color=#3366CC>tetrahydrofuran</color> (THF) or ethylene glycol dimethyl ether (1,2-dimethoxyethane) are avoided in industrial
processes.
Lewis bases

Ethers serve as <color=#3366CC>Lewis bases</color>. For instance, <color=#3366CC>diethyl ether</color> forms a <color=#3366CC>complex</color> with <color=#3366CC>boron trifluoride</color>, i.e. borane diethyl
etherate (BF3*O(CH2CH3)2). Ethers also coordinate to the <color=#3366CC>Mg</color> center in Grignard reagents. <color=#3366CC>Tetrahydrofuran</color> is more
basic than <color=#3366CC>acyclic</color> ethers. It forms with many complexes.
Alpha-halogenation
This reactivity is similar to the tendency of ethers with alpha hydrogen atoms to form peroxides. Reaction with chlorine
produces alpha-chloroethers.
Synthesis
Ethers can be prepared by several methods.x
Dehydration of alcohols
The dehydration of <color=#3366CC>alcohols</color> affords ethers:
This direct nucleophilic substitution reaction requires elevated temperatures (about 125 °C), and an acid catalyst,
usually sulfuric acid. The method is effective for generating symmetrical or cyclic ethers, but not asymmetric, acyclic
ethers. Either OH can be protonated, which would give a mixture of products.
Industrially, <color=#3366CC>diethyl ether</color> is produced from ethanol this way.
The dehydration route often requires conditions incompatible with delicate molecules. Elimination reactions compete
with dehydration of the alcohol: R–CH2–CH2(OH) R–CH=CH2 + H2O
Electrophilic addition of alcohols to alkenes
Alcohols add to electrophilically activated <color=#3366CC>alkenes</color>. The method is atom-economical: <color=#3366CC>R2C=CR2</color> + R–OH
R2CH–C(–O–R)–R2 <color=#3366CC>Acid</color> <color=#3366CC>catalysis</color> is required for this reaction. Commercially important ethers prepared in this way are
derived from isobutene or isoamylene, which protonate to give relatively stable carbocations. Using ethanol and
methanol with these two alkenes, four fuel-grade ethers are produced: methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), methyl tert-amyl
ether (TAME), ethyl tert-butyl ether (ETBE), and ethyl tert-amyl ether (TAEE).
Solid acid catalysts are typically used to promote this reaction.
Ethoxylation and related epoxide ring-opening reactions
Many ethers, ethoxylates and crown ethers, are produced by ring-opening of epoxides.
Williamson and Ullmann ether syntheses
<color=#3366CC>Nucleophilic displacement</color> of <color=#3366CC>alkyl halides</color> by alkoxides R–ONa + R′–X R–O–R′ + Na<color=#3366CC>X</color> The Williamson ether synthesis
involves treatment of a parent <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color> with a strong <color=#3366CC>base</color> to form the alkoxide, followed by addition of an appropriate
<color=#3366CC>aliphatic compound</color> bearing a suitable <color=#3366CC>leaving group</color> (R–X). Although popular in textbooks, the method is often
impractical on scale because it cogenerates significant waste and the harsh conditions can be incompatible with
sensitive functional groups.. Carboxymethyl cellulose is prepared by the Williamson method by alkylation of cellulose
with chloroacetic acid. Glycidyl ethers are also prepared industrially by the Williamson method, starting from
epichlorohydrin.
Suitable leaving groups (X) include <color=#3366CC>iodide</color>, <color=#3366CC>bromide</color>, or sulfonates. This method usually does not work well for aryl
halides (e.g. bromobenzene, see Ullmann condensation below). Likewise, this method only gives the best yields for
primary halides. Secondary and tertiary halides are prone to undergo E2 elimination on exposure to the basic alkoxide
anion used in the reaction due to steric hindrance from the large alkyl groups.
In a related reaction, alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic displacement by phenoxides. The R–X cannot be used to react
with the alcohol. However phenols can be used to replace the alcohol while maintaining the alkyl halide. Since phenols
are acidic, they readily react with a strong <color=#3366CC>base</color> like <color=#3366CC>sodium hydroxide</color> to form phenoxide ions. The phenoxide ion will
then substitute the –X group in the alkyl halide, forming an ether with an aryl group attached to it in a reaction with an
<color=#3366CC>SN2</color> mechanism.
C6H5OH + OH C6H5–O + H2O C6H5–O + R–X C6H5OR
The Ullmann condensation is similar to the Williamson method except that the substrate is an aryl halide. Such
reactions generally require a catalyst, such as copper.
